sections.heading: Subatomic Particles
sections.body: Atoms consist of three subatomic particles. Protons have a positive charge and are located in the nucleus; the number of protons defines the element (atomic number Z). Neutrons have no charge and are also in the nucleus; they contribute to atomic mass. Electrons have a negative charge and orbit the nucleus in electron clouds. The mass number (A) equals protons plus neutrons. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.

sections.heading: Electron Configuration
sections.body: Electrons occupy orbitals described by quantum numbers. The principal quantum number (n) indicates energy level. The angular momentum quantum number (l) indicates orbital shape (s, p, d, f). The magnetic quantum number (ml) indicates orbital orientation. The spin quantum number (ms) is +1/2 or -1/2. The Aufbau principle states electrons fill lowest energy orbitals first. The Pauli exclusion principle says no two electrons can have identical quantum numbers. Hund's rule states electrons fill degenerate orbitals singly before pairing.

sections.heading: Periodic Trends
sections.body: The periodic table organizes elements by atomic number. Periods are horizontal rows; groups are vertical columns. Key periodic trends: atomic radius decreases across a period (increasing nuclear charge) and increases down a group (more electron shells). Ionization energy increases across a period and decreases down a group. Electronegativity (tendency to attract electrons) increases across a period and decreases down a group. Electron affinity generally becomes more negative across a period.

sections.heading: Historical Atomic Models
sections.body: Dalton proposed that atoms are indivisible solid spheres. Thomson's plum pudding model placed electrons in a positive matrix. Rutherford's gold foil experiment revealed a dense positive nucleus. Bohr's model placed electrons in fixed circular orbits with quantized energy levels. The modern quantum mechanical model describes electrons as probability clouds (orbitals) based on Schrodinger's wave equation. Heisenberg's uncertainty principle states you cannot simultaneously know both the position and momentum of an electron precisely.

sections.heading: Ionic Bonds
sections.body: Ionic bonds form when electrons are transferred from a metal to a nonmetal, creating oppositely charged ions that attract. Cations are positively charged ions (metals lose electrons). Anions are negatively charged ions (nonmetals gain electrons). Ionic compounds form crystal lattices, have high melting points, conduct electricity when dissolved or molten, and are generally soluble in water. Lattice energy measures the strength of ionic bonds.

sections.heading: Covalent Bonds
sections.body: Covalent bonds form when atoms share electrons, typically between nonmetals. Single bonds share one pair, double bonds share two pairs, and triple bonds share three pairs. Bond energy and bond length are inversely related: triple bonds are shortest and strongest. Polar covalent bonds have unequal sharing due to electronegativity differences. Nonpolar covalent bonds have equal sharing. Lewis structures show bonding and lone pair electrons. The octet rule states atoms tend to achieve eight valence electrons.

sections.heading: VSEPR Theory and Molecular Geometry
sections.body: VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) theory predicts molecular geometry based on minimizing electron pair repulsion. Common geometries: linear (2 bonding, 0 lone pairs, 180 degrees), trigonal planar (3 bonding, 0 lone, 120 degrees), tetrahedral (4 bonding, 0 lone, 109.5 degrees), bent (2 bonding, 1-2 lone), trigonal pyramidal (3 bonding, 1 lone). Molecular polarity depends on both bond polarity and molecular geometry. Symmetric molecules can be nonpolar despite having polar bonds.

sections.heading: Intermolecular Forces
sections.body: Intermolecular forces (IMFs) are attractions between molecules. London dispersion forces (weakest) exist in all molecules and increase with molar mass. Dipole-dipole forces occur between polar molecules. Hydrogen bonds (strongest IMF) occur when H is bonded to N, O, or F and interacts with another N, O, or F. IMFs determine physical properties: stronger IMFs mean higher boiling points, higher viscosity, and greater surface tension. Metallic bonding involves a sea of delocalized electrons shared among metal atoms.

sections.heading: The Mole Concept
sections.body: A mole is 6.022 x 10^23 particles (Avogadro's number). The molar mass of an element equals its atomic mass in grams per mole. For compounds, molar mass is the sum of all atomic masses in the formula. Molar volume of an ideal gas at STP (0 degrees C, 1 atm) is 22.4 L/mol. Conversions between grams, moles, and particles use molar mass and Avogadro's number as conversion factors.

sections.heading: Balancing Chemical Equations
sections.body: The law of conservation of mass states that matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. Chemical equations must be balanced so that atoms of each element are equal on both sides. Coefficients (not subscripts) are adjusted to balance equations. Types of reactions: synthesis (A + B -> AB), decomposition (AB -> A + B), single replacement (A + BC -> AC + B), double replacement (AB + CD -> AD + CB), and combustion (hydrocarbon + O2 -> CO2 + H2O).

sections.heading: Stoichiometric Calculations
sections.body: Stoichiometry uses mole ratios from balanced equations to convert between amounts of reactants and products. The general approach: convert given quantity to moles, use mole ratio to find moles of desired substance, then convert to required units. The limiting reagent is the reactant that runs out first, determining the theoretical yield. Excess reagent is left over. Percent yield equals (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100%.

sections.heading: Oxidation-Reduction Reactions
sections.body: Redox reactions involve transfer of electrons. Oxidation is loss of electrons (increase in oxidation number). Reduction is gain of electrons (decrease in oxidation number). The mnemonic OIL RIG helps remember: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain. The oxidizing agent is reduced (gains electrons). The reducing agent is oxidized (loses electrons). Oxidation numbers follow specific rules: free elements are 0, monatomic ions equal their charge, and oxygen is usually -2, hydrogen is usually +1.

sections.heading: Gas Laws
sections.body: Boyle's law: at constant temperature, pressure and volume are inversely proportional (P1V1 = P2V2). Charles's law: at constant pressure, volume and temperature are directly proportional (V1/T1 = V2/T2). Gay-Lussac's law: at constant volume, pressure and temperature are directly proportional. The combined gas law merges all three. The ideal gas law is PV = nRT, where R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K). Dalton's law of partial pressures states total pressure equals the sum of individual gas pressures.

sections.heading: Phase Changes
sections.body: Matter exists as solid, liquid, gas, or plasma. Phase transitions: melting (solid to liquid), freezing (liquid to solid), vaporization (liquid to gas), condensation (gas to liquid), sublimation (solid to gas), and deposition (gas to solid). During phase changes, temperature remains constant as energy goes into breaking or forming intermolecular forces. Phase diagrams show temperature and pressure conditions for each phase. The triple point is where all three phases coexist. The critical point is where liquid and gas become indistinguishable.

sections.heading: Solutions and Concentration
sections.body: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent. Concentration can be expressed as molarity (moles of solute per liter of solution), molality (moles of solute per kilogram of solvent), percent by mass, or parts per million (ppm). 'Like dissolves like': polar solvents dissolve polar solutes, nonpolar solvents dissolve nonpolar solutes. Solubility generally increases with temperature for solids and decreases for gases. Henry's law states that gas solubility is proportional to partial pressure.

sections.heading: Colligative Properties
sections.body: Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles, not their identity. Boiling point elevation: adding solute raises the boiling point. Freezing point depression: adding solute lowers the freezing point. Vapor pressure lowering (Raoult's law): adding solute decreases vapor pressure. Osmotic pressure drives solvent flow across a semipermeable membrane from low to high solute concentration. The van't Hoff factor (i) accounts for dissociation of ionic compounds in solution.

sections.heading: Acid-Base Theories
sections.body: Arrhenius acids produce H+ in water; Arrhenius bases produce OH-. Bronsted-Lowry acids are proton donors; Bronsted-Lowry bases are proton acceptors. Lewis acids are electron pair acceptors; Lewis bases are electron pair donors. Strong acids (HCl, HNO3, H2SO4, HBr, HI, HClO4) completely dissociate. Weak acids partially dissociate and have an equilibrium constant Ka. Strong bases (NaOH, KOH) completely dissociate. Weak bases have Kb.

sections.heading: pH and Buffers
sections.body: pH = -log[H+], where [H+] is the hydrogen ion concentration. Neutral pH is 7. Acidic solutions have pH < 7; basic solutions have pH > 7. pOH = -log[OH-]. pH + pOH = 14 at 25 degrees C. The ion product of water: Kw = [H+][OH-] = 1.0 x 10^-14. Buffers resist changes in pH and consist of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or weak base and its conjugate acid). The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]).

sections.heading: Chemical Equilibrium
sections.body: Chemical equilibrium occurs when forward and reverse reaction rates are equal. The equilibrium constant K = [products]/[reactants], each raised to their stoichiometric coefficients. A large K favors products; a small K favors reactants. Le Chatelier's principle states that if a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts to counteract the change. Adding reactant shifts right; adding product shifts left. Increasing temperature shifts toward the endothermic direction. Changing pressure affects gaseous equilibria.

sections.heading: Titration and Solubility Equilibria
sections.body: Titration determines the concentration of an unknown solution by reacting it with a known solution. The equivalence point is where moles of acid equal moles of base. Indicators change color near the equivalence point. Strong acid-strong base titrations have an equivalence point at pH 7. Weak acid-strong base titrations have equivalence points above 7. The solubility product constant (Ksp) describes the equilibrium for slightly soluble ionic compounds. The common ion effect decreases solubility when a shared ion is already present.

sections.heading: Enthalpy and Hess's Law
sections.body: Enthalpy (H) is the heat content of a system at constant pressure. An exothermic reaction releases heat (negative delta H). An endothermic reaction absorbs heat (positive delta H). Hess's law states that the total enthalpy change is independent of the path taken. Standard enthalpy of formation (delta Hf) is the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements. Bond energies can estimate delta H: energy required to break bonds minus energy released forming bonds.

sections.heading: Entropy and Gibbs Free Energy
sections.body: Entropy (S) measures disorder or randomness. The second law of thermodynamics states that entropy of the universe always increases. Entropy increases when: solids become liquids or gases, temperature increases, or the number of particles increases. Gibbs free energy (G) combines enthalpy and entropy: delta G = delta H - T(delta S). A reaction is spontaneous when delta G < 0, nonspontaneous when delta G > 0, and at equilibrium when delta G = 0. The relationship delta G = -RT ln K connects free energy to the equilibrium constant.

sections.heading: Reaction Rates
sections.body: Reaction rate measures how quickly reactants are consumed or products are formed. Factors affecting rate: concentration (higher concentration increases rate), temperature (higher temperature increases rate), surface area (more surface area increases rate), and catalysts (lower activation energy). The rate law expresses rate as k[A]^m[B]^n, where k is the rate constant and m, n are reaction orders determined experimentally. The Arrhenius equation relates the rate constant to temperature and activation energy: k = Ae^(-Ea/RT).

sections.heading: Reaction Mechanisms and Catalysis
sections.body: A reaction mechanism is a series of elementary steps that describe how a reaction occurs. The rate-determining step is the slowest step and determines the overall rate. Intermediates are formed in one step and consumed in another. The molecularity of an elementary step is the number of reactant molecules involved (unimolecular, bimolecular). Catalysts speed up reactions by providing an alternative pathway with lower activation energy. Enzymes are biological catalysts. Homogeneous catalysts are in the same phase as reactants; heterogeneous catalysts are in a different phase.

sections.heading: Redox Reactions and Half-Reactions
sections.body: Electrochemistry studies the interconversion of chemical and electrical energy through redox reactions. Oxidation occurs at the anode (loses electrons), and reduction occurs at the cathode (gains electrons). Half-reactions separate oxidation and reduction processes. Balancing redox equations in acidic solution uses H+ and H2O; in basic solution, use OH- and H2O. The standard reduction potential (E°) measures the tendency of a species to be reduced. A more positive E° indicates a stronger oxidizing agent.

sections.heading: Galvanic Cells
sections.body: Galvanic (voltaic) cells convert chemical energy to electrical energy spontaneously. The cell consists of two half-cells connected by a salt bridge, which maintains electrical neutrality. The cell potential E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode. A positive E°cell indicates a spontaneous reaction. The relationship between cell potential and free energy is delta G = -nFE, where n is moles of electrons and F is Faraday's constant (96,485 C/mol). Common galvanic cells include the Daniell cell (zinc-copper) and the lead-acid battery.

sections.heading: Electrolytic Cells
sections.body: Electrolytic cells use electrical energy to drive non-spontaneous redox reactions. Examples include electroplating, purification of metals, and production of chemicals. The anode is still where oxidation occurs, but in an electrolytic cell it is connected to the positive terminal. Water can be electrolyzed into hydrogen and oxygen gases. Faraday's laws of electrolysis relate the amount of substance produced to the current and time: mass is proportional to charge passed (Q = It). Electrorefining purifies metals like copper.

sections.heading: Batteries and Fuel Cells
sections.body: Batteries store chemical energy and convert it to electrical energy. Primary batteries (alkaline, zinc-carbon) are single-use. Secondary batteries (lead-acid, lithium-ion, nickel-metal hydride) are rechargeable. Lithium-ion batteries have high energy density and are used in portable electronics and electric vehicles. Fuel cells continuously generate electricity from reactants supplied externally. Hydrogen fuel cells combine H2 and O2 to produce electricity, with water as the only byproduct. The Nernst equation relates cell potential to concentrations: E = E° - (RT/nF)ln(Q).

sections.heading: Hydrocarbons
sections.body: Hydrocarbons contain only carbon and hydrogen. Alkanes have single bonds (CnH2n+2) and are saturated. Alkenes have at least one double bond (CnH2n). Alkynes have at least one triple bond (CnH2n-2). Aromatic hydrocarbons contain benzene rings with delocalized pi electrons. IUPAC nomenclature uses prefixes for carbon chain length (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-) and suffixes indicating bond type (-ane, -ene, -yne). Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different connectivity.

sections.heading: Functional Groups
sections.body: Functional groups are specific atom arrangements that determine chemical properties. Alcohols have -OH groups (nomenclature: -ol). Aldehydes have a carbonyl at the end of a chain (-al). Ketones have a carbonyl within the chain (-one). Carboxylic acids have -COOH groups (-oic acid). Esters form from carboxylic acids and alcohols (-oate). Amines contain nitrogen (-amine). Ethers have an oxygen between two carbons. Functional groups undergo characteristic reactions.

sections.heading: Isomerism
sections.body: Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures. Structural isomers differ in connectivity. Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but different spatial arrangements. Geometric (cis-trans) isomers differ in arrangement around a double bond or ring. Optical isomers (enantiomers) are non-superimposable mirror images. Chiral molecules lack a plane of symmetry and rotate plane-polarized light. A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of both enantiomers. Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images.

sections.heading: Organic Reactions
sections.body: Addition reactions add atoms across a double or triple bond (e.g., hydrogenation, halogenation). Substitution reactions replace one atom or group with another (e.g., halogenation of alkanes). Elimination reactions remove atoms to form double or triple bonds (e.g., dehydration of alcohols). Condensation reactions join molecules with loss of a small molecule (often water). Polymerization joins monomers to form polymers. Oxidation of alcohols produces aldehydes or ketones. Reduction of aldehydes or ketones produces alcohols.

sections.heading: Radioactive Decay
sections.body: Radioactive decay is the spontaneous emission of particles or energy from unstable nuclei. Alpha decay emits an alpha particle (helium-4 nucleus), reducing atomic number by 2 and mass number by 4. Beta-minus decay converts a neutron to a proton, emitting an electron and antineutrino. Beta-plus decay converts a proton to a neutron, emitting a positron and neutrino. Gamma decay emits high-energy photons without changing atomic or mass number. Electron capture occurs when a nucleus captures an inner electron, converting a proton to a neutron.

sections.heading: Half-Life and Decay Kinetics
sections.body: Half-life (t1/2) is the time for half of a radioactive sample to decay. Radioactive decay follows first-order kinetics: N(t) = N0 * e^(-lambda*t), where lambda is the decay constant. The relationship between half-life and decay constant is t1/2 = ln(2)/lambda = 0.693/lambda. Carbon-14 dating uses the decay of C-14 (half-life 5,730 years) to date organic materials up to about 50,000 years old. Uranium-lead dating is used for much older rocks. Activity is measured in becquerels (decays per second) or curies.

sections.heading: Nuclear Fission and Fusion
sections.body: Nuclear fission splits heavy nuclei into lighter nuclei, releasing energy. U-235 and Pu-239 are fissile materials. A neutron strikes the nucleus, causing it to split into two fission fragments plus neutrons. These neutrons can trigger more fissions in a chain reaction. Nuclear reactors control the chain reaction using control rods and moderators. Nuclear fusion combines light nuclei into heavier nuclei, releasing even more energy per unit mass. The Sun fuses hydrogen into helium. Fusion requires extremely high temperatures to overcome electrostatic repulsion.

sections.heading: Applications of Nuclear Chemistry
sections.body: Medical applications include PET scans (positron emission tomography), radiation therapy for cancer, and radioactive tracers for diagnosis. Nuclear medicine uses isotopes like Tc-99m, I-131, and Co-60. Industrial applications include radiography for testing welds, gauging thickness, and sterilizing equipment. Nuclear power plants generate electricity through controlled fission. Challenges include radioactive waste disposal and safety concerns. Nuclear weapons use uncontrolled fission or fusion. Radiation exposure is measured in grays (absorbed dose) and sieverts (biological effect).

sections.heading: Properties of Transition Metals
sections.body: Transition metals occupy the d-block of the periodic table (groups 3-12). They have partially filled d orbitals and exhibit variable oxidation states (e.g., Fe2+ and Fe3+). Transition metals form colored compounds due to d-d electron transitions. They often act as catalysts due to their ability to change oxidation states. They have high melting points, high densities, and good electrical and thermal conductivity. Lanthanides and actinides are f-block elements with partially filled f orbitals.

sections.heading: Coordination Compounds
sections.body: Coordination compounds contain a central metal ion bonded to ligands. Ligands are Lewis bases that donate electron pairs. The coordination number is the number of ligand donor atoms bonded to the metal (commonly 4 or 6). Monodentate ligands (H2O, NH3, Cl-) bind through one atom. Bidentate ligands (ethylenediamine) bind through two atoms. Polydentate ligands (EDTA) bind through multiple atoms. Common geometries include tetrahedral (coordination number 4), square planar (4), and octahedral (6).

sections.heading: Nomenclature and Isomerism
sections.body: Coordination compound nomenclature lists ligands alphabetically before the metal. Anionic ligands end in -o (chloro, hydroxo). Neutral ligands keep their names (except aqua for H2O, ammine for NH3). The oxidation state of the metal is given in Roman numerals. Geometric isomers include cis (similar groups adjacent) and trans (similar groups opposite). Optical isomers (enantiomers) are non-superimposable mirror images. Linkage isomers have ligands that can bind through different atoms (e.g., NO2- can bind through N or O).

sections.heading: Crystal Field Theory
sections.body: Crystal field theory explains the bonding, color, and magnetism of coordination compounds. Ligands create an electrostatic field that splits d orbitals into different energy levels. In an octahedral field, d orbitals split into lower-energy t2g and higher-energy eg levels. The energy difference is the crystal field splitting energy (delta). Strong-field ligands (CN-, CO) cause large splitting and favor low-spin complexes (electrons pair in lower orbitals). Weak-field ligands (I-, Br-) cause small splitting and favor high-spin complexes. Color arises from d-d transitions absorbing specific wavelengths.

sections.heading: Infrared Spectroscopy
sections.body: Infrared (IR) spectroscopy measures the absorption of infrared radiation by molecular vibrations. Different functional groups absorb at characteristic frequencies (wavenumbers, cm-1). O-H stretches appear at 3200-3600 cm-1 (broad for alcohols). N-H stretches appear at 3300-3500 cm-1. C=O stretches appear at 1650-1750 cm-1. C-H stretches appear at 2850-3000 cm-1. The fingerprint region (below 1500 cm-1) is unique to each molecule. IR spectroscopy identifies functional groups and confirms molecular structure.

sections.heading: UV-Visible Spectroscopy
sections.body: UV-Visible spectroscopy measures the absorption of ultraviolet and visible light by electrons transitioning between energy levels. Conjugated systems and aromatic compounds absorb strongly in the UV region. The Beer-Lambert law relates absorbance to concentration: A = epsilon*b*c, where epsilon is the molar absorptivity, b is path length, and c is concentration. UV-Vis spectroscopy determines concentration, measures reaction rates, and studies electronic structure. Colored compounds absorb in the visible region (400-700 nm). The color observed is complementary to the color absorbed.

sections.heading: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy
sections.body: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) spectroscopy detects nuclei with non-zero spin (1H, 13C, 31P) in a magnetic field. Proton NMR (1H-NMR) is most common. Chemical shift (delta, in ppm) indicates the electronic environment. Equivalent protons appear at the same chemical shift. Integration gives the relative number of protons. Splitting patterns arise from spin-spin coupling with neighboring protons (n+1 rule). A singlet has no neighboring protons, doublet has one, triplet has two, quartet has three. Carbon-13 NMR provides information about carbon environments.

sections.heading: Mass Spectrometry
sections.body: Mass spectrometry (MS) measures the mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) of ions. A sample is ionized, producing a molecular ion (M+). Fragmentation produces smaller ions characteristic of the molecular structure. The molecular ion peak gives the molecular mass. Isotope patterns help identify elements (chlorine and bromine have distinctive patterns). High-resolution MS determines molecular formulas. MS is coupled with chromatography (GC-MS, LC-MS) for complex mixture analysis. Tandem MS (MS/MS) provides structural information through successive fragmentation.

sections.heading: Addition Polymers
sections.body: Addition polymerization (chain-growth polymerization) occurs when monomers with double bonds link together without loss of atoms. The process involves initiation (forming a reactive species), propagation (adding monomers to the chain), and termination. Common addition polymers include polyethylene (PE) from ethylene, polypropylene (PP) from propylene, polystyrene (PS) from styrene, and polyvinyl chloride (PVC) from vinyl chloride. High-density polyethylene (HDPE) is linear and strong. Low-density polyethylene (LDPE) is branched and flexible. Teflon (PTFE) is made from tetrafluoroethylene.

sections.heading: Condensation Polymers
sections.body: Condensation polymerization (step-growth polymerization) occurs when monomers join with loss of a small molecule (usually water). Polyesters form from diols and dicarboxylic acids (e.g., PET from ethylene glycol and terephthalic acid). Polyamides form from diamines and dicarboxylic acids (e.g., nylon-6,6). Polycarbonates are used in eyeglass lenses and CDs. Polyurethanes form from diols and diisocyanates, used in foams and coatings. Natural condensation polymers include proteins (amino acids) and cellulose (glucose).

sections.heading: Polymer Properties
sections.body: Polymer properties depend on molecular structure and intermolecular forces. Thermoplastics soften when heated and can be reshaped (PE, PP, PS, PVC). Thermosets form cross-linked networks and cannot be reshaped after curing (epoxy, phenol-formaldehyde). Elastomers are flexible polymers that can be stretched (rubber, silicone). Crystallinity increases strength and rigidity. Branching decreases crystallinity and density. Cross-linking increases strength and heat resistance. Glass transition temperature (Tg) is where a polymer changes from brittle to flexible.

sections.heading: Advanced Materials
sections.body: Composites combine two or more materials to achieve superior properties. Fiberglass combines glass fibers in a polymer matrix. Carbon fiber composites are lightweight and strong, used in aerospace and sports equipment. Ceramics are inorganic, non-metallic materials with high melting points, hardness, and brittleness. Semiconductors have conductivity between conductors and insulators, essential for electronics. Nanomaterials have dimensions of 1-100 nm and exhibit unique properties. Carbon nanotubes and graphene have exceptional strength and conductivity. Smart materials respond to external stimuli (shape-memory alloys, self-healing polymers).

sections.heading: Air Pollution
sections.body: Major air pollutants include particulate matter (PM2.5 and PM10), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2), nitrogen oxides (NOx), ozone (O3), and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). Photochemical smog forms when NOx and VOCs react in sunlight, producing ozone. Acid rain forms when SO2 and NOx dissolve in atmospheric water, producing sulfuric and nitric acids. Acid rain damages forests, lakes, and buildings. The Clean Air Act regulates air pollutants. Catalytic converters in vehicles reduce CO, NOx, and hydrocarbons.

sections.heading: Ozone Depletion
sections.body: The ozone layer in the stratosphere absorbs harmful UV-B radiation. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) release chlorine atoms in the stratosphere. Chlorine catalytically destroys ozone: Cl + O3 -> ClO + O2, then ClO + O -> Cl + O2, regenerating chlorine. One chlorine atom can destroy thousands of ozone molecules. The Antarctic ozone hole appears each spring. The Montreal Protocol (1987) phased out CFCs and other ozone-depleting substances. Replacement compounds include HFCs (hydrochlorofluorocarbons) and HFCs (hydrofluorocarbons).

sections.heading: Water Pollution and Treatment
sections.body: Water pollutants include pathogens, organic matter (measured by BOD - biochemical oxygen demand), nutrients (nitrogen and phosphorus causing eutrophication), heavy metals (lead, mercury), and synthetic chemicals (pesticides, pharmaceuticals). Eutrophication occurs when excess nutrients promote algal blooms, which die and decompose, depleting oxygen. Water treatment includes coagulation and flocculation, sedimentation, filtration, and disinfection (chlorination, UV, ozone). Wastewater treatment involves primary treatment (physical removal), secondary treatment (biological decomposition), and tertiary treatment (nutrient removal).

sections.heading: Green Chemistry
sections.body: Green chemistry designs chemical products and processes to reduce or eliminate hazardous substances. The 12 principles include preventing waste, designing safer chemicals, using renewable feedstocks, designing for energy efficiency, using catalysts, and designing for degradation. Atom economy measures the efficiency of a reaction: (mass of desired product / total mass of products) x 100%. Green solvents include water, supercritical CO2, and ionic liquids. Biocatalysis uses enzymes for chemical transformations. Green chemistry reduces environmental impact and improves sustainability.

sections.heading: Carbohydrates
sections.body: Carbohydrates have the general formula (CH2O)n. Monosaccharides are simple sugars (glucose, fructose, ribose). Disaccharides form from two monosaccharides via glycosidic bonds (sucrose = glucose + fructose, lactose = glucose + galactose, maltose = glucose + glucose). Polysaccharides are polymers: starch and glycogen store energy, cellulose provides structure in plants, and chitin provides structure in arthropods. Glucose exists in linear and cyclic forms (alpha and beta anomers). Carbohydrates provide energy (4 kcal/g) and structural support.

sections.heading: Lipids
sections.body: Lipids are hydrophobic molecules including fats, oils, waxes, and steroids. Fatty acids have a carboxylic acid head and a long hydrocarbon tail. Saturated fatty acids have no double bonds; unsaturated fatty acids have one or more double bonds. Triglycerides (triacylglycerols) consist of glycerol esterified to three fatty acids, serving as energy storage (9 kcal/g). Phospholipids form cell membranes with hydrophilic heads and hydrophobic tails. Steroids have a four-ring structure (cholesterol, testosterone, estrogen). Lipids are insoluble in water but soluble in nonpolar solvents.

sections.heading: Proteins
sections.body: Proteins are polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds. There are 20 standard amino acids, each with an amino group, carboxyl group, and unique side chain (R group). Protein structure has four levels: primary (amino acid sequence), secondary (alpha helix, beta sheet stabilized by hydrogen bonds), tertiary (3D folding stabilized by disulfide bonds, ionic interactions, hydrophobic effects), and quaternary (multiple polypeptide subunits). Enzymes catalyze biochemical reactions. Denaturation disrupts protein structure through heat, pH changes, or chemicals.

sections.heading: Nucleic Acids and Metabolism
sections.body: Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) are polymers of nucleotides. Each nucleotide has a sugar (ribose or deoxyribose), a phosphate group, and a nitrogenous base. DNA bases are adenine, thymine, guanine, cytosine. RNA uses uracil instead of thymine. DNA is double-stranded with complementary base pairing (A-T, G-C). Metabolism includes catabolism (breaking down molecules for energy) and anabolism (building molecules). Cellular respiration converts glucose to ATP. Glycolysis breaks glucose into pyruvate. The citric acid cycle produces NADH and FADH2. The electron transport chain produces most ATP.

sections.heading: The Haber Process
sections.body: The Haber process synthesizes ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen: N2(g) + 3H2(g) <-> 2NH3(g). The reaction is exothermic (delta H = -92 kJ/mol) and produces fewer moles of gas. According to Le Chatelier's principle, high pressure (150-250 atm) favors ammonia production. Lower temperatures favor ammonia but slow the reaction, so a compromise temperature of 400-500 degrees C is used with an iron catalyst. Ammonia is used to produce fertilizers (ammonium nitrate, urea), explosives, and nitric acid. The Haber process enabled large-scale food production.

sections.heading: The Contact Process
sections.body: The contact process produces sulfuric acid, the most widely produced industrial chemical. Step 1: Sulfur or sulfide ores are burned to produce SO2. Step 2: SO2 is oxidized to SO3 using a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst: 2SO2 + O2 <-> 2SO3. The reaction is exothermic, so lower temperatures favor SO3, but 450 degrees C is used for practical rates. High pressure is not needed despite favoring products. Step 3: SO3 is dissolved in concentrated H2SO4 (forming oleum), then diluted with water. Sulfuric acid is used in fertilizers, petroleum refining, and chemical manufacturing.

sections.heading: Petroleum Refining
sections.body: Petroleum is a complex mixture of hydrocarbons. Fractional distillation separates crude oil into fractions based on boiling points: refinery gas, gasoline (naphtha), kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil, and bitumen. Cracking breaks large hydrocarbons into smaller, more useful molecules using heat and catalysts (catalytic cracking) or steam (steam cracking). Reforming converts straight-chain hydrocarbons into branched and aromatic compounds, increasing octane number. Alkylation combines small molecules into larger gasoline-range molecules. Hydrotreating removes sulfur, nitrogen, and metals.

sections.heading: Other Industrial Processes
sections.body: The Ostwald process produces nitric acid from ammonia: ammonia is oxidized to NO using a platinum catalyst, NO is oxidized to NO2, and NO2 dissolves in water to form HNO3. The Solvay process produces sodium carbonate (soda ash) from salt, limestone, and ammonia. The Chloralkali process electrolyzes brine to produce chlorine, hydrogen, and sodium hydroxide. The Hall-Heroult process produces aluminum by electrolysis of molten aluminum oxide in cryolite. The Frasch process extracts sulfur from underground deposits using superheated water.
